raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old Japanese man was admitted to our hospital because of high-grade fever with transient consciousness disorder and double vision. He had no medical history throughout his childhood and adolescence but continued to have repeated fever and productive cough since the age of 25. He also presented with stomatitis and dental caries. His mother had a history of disseminated cryptococcosis and died from chronic hepatitis C virus infection. His younger brother had been clinically diagnosed with CMCD for having recurrent and refractory cutaneous candidiasis although no genetic analysis has been performed on his dissent.
Physical examination on the admission revealed that the majority of his teeth were corroded, and that he had white moss throughout his mouth. A nuchal stiffness was noted with right abductor paralysis. His chest computed tomography (CT) showed bronchiectasis and multiple granular shadows randomly distributed in the bilateral lower and middle lobes, thin-walled cysts predominantly in both upper lobes, and consolidation in the lower left lobe ( Figure 1 ). Cryptococcus neoformans was isolated from his blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples and was also detected in liver and lung biopsies. Accordingly, he was diagnosed with disseminated cryptococcosis with meningitis and oral and cutaneous candidiasis.
The patient was treated with a combination therapy of liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine for 8 weeks. Consequently, his respiratory symptoms and neurological abnormalities resolved. The cryptococcal antigen titers in his cerebrospinal fluid decreased from 1,024 times to 32. His chest CT on day 44 of the treatment showed that the granular shadows and consolidation entirely improved, but the bronchiectases in his right middle lobe and left lingular segment remained. The antifungal treatment was then switched to oral fluconazole, and the disease did not recur for one year.
The patient was suspected of having primary immunodeficiency because of the present clinical course and his family history. We sequenced the patient's CMCD-related genes and found a previously recognized heterozygous missense mutation in the coiled-coil domain of the STAT1 gene (c.820C>T, p.R274W). The same mutation was also detected in his younger brother. The monocytes of the patient showed hyper-phosphorylation of STAT1 after stimulation with interferon-gamma ( Figure 2 ). Based on these results, the patient was diagnosed with STAT1 GOF.
Additionally, the patient presented with low serum IgG and IgA levels [IgG: 2.36 g/L, normal range (NR): 8.61-17.47 g/L; IgA: 0.05 g/L, NR: 0.93-3.93; IgM: 0.92 g/L, NR: 0.33-1.83]. Surface marker analyses revealed that 72.3% (NR: 54.3-81.9%) of his peripheral lymphocytes comprised CD3+ cells with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 32.8 (NR: 24.3-49.7%)/36.2 (NR: 18.4-49.0%), and that 0.1% (NR: 2.9-20.1%) comprised CD19+ cells ( Table 1 ). Peripheral blood lymphocyte responsiveness to phytohemagglutinin was normal (Stimulation Index: 281, NR: 254-388). The level of T-cell receptor excision circles was 2.06 x 102 copies/mugDNA [NR: 3.4 +- 3.6 x 102 copies/mug DNA ], whereas both those of the coding joint and signal joint kappa-deleting recombination excision circles were undetermined. We then investigated the cause of hypogammaglobulinemia and B-cell lymphopenia. The B-cell differentiation was blocked in the stages between VpreB+IgMlow (pre-B1b) cells and VpreB-IgMlow (pre-B2) cells in the bone marrow sample obtained three months after the onset of cryptococcosis ( Figure 3 ). Human immunodeficiency virus-RNA and Epstein-Barr virus- and cytomegalovirus-DNA were undetectable by polymerase chain reaction. No pathogenic variants in antibody deficiency-causing genes listed in the 2017 Primary Immunodeficiency Diseases Committee Report on Inborn Errors of Immunity were detected using the target panel sequence. The reduction in the peripheral B-cell counts had persisted even after the patient's recovery from cryptococcosis ( Table 1 ). His prolonged respiratory symptoms did not recur upon regular subcutaneous immunoglobulin infusion to maintain a trough level of >7.0 g/L.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old Japanese man presented with high-grade fever, transient disturbance of consciousness, and diplopia on a 5-year background of recurrent fever and productive cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Since age 25, the patient had experienced repeated episodes of fever, productive cough, stomatitis, and severe dental caries. He was admitted with acute high-grade fever, transient altered consciousness, and double vision.
subjective.past_medical_history: 5-year history of recurrent respiratory infections, stomatitis, and dental caries. Family history significant for his mother having had disseminated cryptococcosis (and dying of chronic HCV) and his younger brother having chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMCD).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, transient consciousness disturbance, diplopia, chronic productive cough, oral thrush/stomatitis, and dental caries.

objective.physical_examination: High-grade fever, nuchal stiffness, right abducens nerve (lateral rectus) palsy, extensive dental caries/corrosion, and thick white oral candidal plaques throughout the oral cavity.
objective.routine_investigations: Hypogammaglobulinemia with low serum IgG (2.36 g/L; normal: 8.61-17.47 g/L) and IgA (0.05 g/L; normal: 0.93-3.93 g/L) and normal IgM (0.92 g/L; normal: 0.33-1.83 g/L); PCR tests for HIV-RNA, EBV-DNA, and CMV-DNA were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT showed bilateral middle/lower lobe bronchiectasis and random granular shadows, bilateral upper lobe thin-walled cysts, and left lower lobe consolidation. Blood and CSF cultures as well as liver and lung biopsies were positive for Cryptococcus neoformans, with initial CSF cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:1,024. Immunological and genetic workup revealed profound B-cell lymphopenia (CD19+ 0.1%; normal: 2.9-20.1%) with arrested bone marrow B-cell differentiation between pre-B1b and pre-B2 stages, undetectable KRECs, normal PHA T-cell proliferation, and a heterozygous gain-of-function (GOF) missense mutation in the STAT1 coiled-coil domain (c.820C>T, p.R274W) with monocyte STAT1 hyper-phosphorylation upon IFN-gamma stimulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans infection (meningitis, fungemia, pneumonia, and hepatitis) and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis secondary to a familial heterozygous STAT1 gain-of-function mutation (c.820C>T, p.R274W) with B-cell differentiation arrest and hypogammaglobulinemia, confirmed by blood/CSF cultures, liver/lung biopsies, CSF CrAg titer (1:1,024), STAT1 genetic sequencing, and flow cytometry. Treated with 8 weeks of IV liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine (resolving neurological/respiratory symptoms and reducing CSF CrAg to 1:32) followed by oral fluconazole maintenance and regular subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement (maintaining IgG trough >7.0 g/L), with no recurrence of cryptococcosis or respiratory infections over 1 year of follow-up.
